issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Grief Reminders' is not well aligned with the indexed trauma of witnessing domestic violence in childhood unless there was also a salient bereavement/loss component. None of the other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal items indicate traumatic loss, so this strategy appears to target a different problem domain than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is hard to reconcile with this patient's age (21), single status, and the rest of the profile unless a specific caretaking or protective role is central to the trauma narrative. The other items emphasize danger sensitivity, helpless coping, and injustice toward perpetrators, but do not support a salient role-failure theme, making this appraisal feel insufficiently grounded in the profile.

vignette: Alejandra's eyes would scan a room, taking in every detail, before she felt comfortable enough to sit. As an animator, her attention to detail was both a gift and a curse. She had grown up witnessing domestic violence between her parents, the sounds of shattering glass and screams still echoing in her mind. The memories of those moments were more real than normal, vivid and alive, making it hard for her to distinguish them from reality. When she saw someone throwing objects, even if it was just a harmless game of catch, Alejandra's heart would racing, transporting her back to the nights she had huddled in her room, listening to the sounds of destruction. The visual cues – photos of her childhood home, or pictures of couples arguing – also triggered these memories. Even certain smells could transport her back to that time and place, like the scent of freshly cooked dinner wafting through the house as the yelling escalated. These triggers would set off a chain reaction in Alejandra's mind. She became increasingly irritable, prone to outbursts when something didn't go according to plan. Her startle response was also heightened – unexpected movements nearby made her react as if she were in danger. To cope with these feelings of hypervigilance, Alejandra would resort to maladaptive strategies: restricting her eating habits to feel a sense of control over her life, avoiding any plans for the future that might seem uncertain or unstable. As she delved deeper into her memories, Alejandra found herself pushing them away before they became too vivid. She couldn't bear the thought of reliving those moments, so she would distract herself with work or other activities. But these blocked memories only seemed to fuel her negative appraisals – she felt helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to her or others. The fact that no one had ever held her father accountable for his actions reinforced this sense of powerlessness. Alejandra's maladaptive strategies also influenced her perception of the world around her. By restricting her eating habits and avoiding future plans, she felt like she could stave off potential dangers or uncertainties. But these behaviors only served to reinforce her memories of the traumatic events – making them feel even more real and present in her life. As an animator, Alejandra's creativity was stifled by her hypervigilance and fear of uncertainty. She found herself avoiding projects that required her to plan too far ahead or collaborate with others. Her irritability had also begun to strain relationships with friends and colleagues. Feeling like she couldn't deal with even the slightest upset made her question whether she could ever truly succeed in her chosen career. Alejandra's journey through these dark memories and maladaptive strategies had left her feeling drained and hopeless. It was this sense of desperation that finally brought her to seek help – a glimmer of recognition that maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this cycle of fear and hypervigilance. She hoped that therapy would provide her with the tools to confront these memories head-on, rather than constantly running from them.
